questions.question: What are clinicians' biggest pain points with documentation?

seeded.answer: Clinicians report that documentation burden is their #1 self-selected contributor to burnout ( [1] ). 52% of physicians specifically ranked documentation burden as the #1 driver of burnout, ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%) [1]. 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours, averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day [1]. A physician participant stated, "I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in." [2].

questions.question: Why didn't physicians trust the ambient scribe's draft notes?

seeded.answer: In early testing, physicians read every line of AI-generated text before accepting it [1][2]. Four out of five participants read every line of AI-generated text before accepting it in this first exposure; none trusted it enough to skim, which undercuts the time-savings premise if that behavior persists post-adoption [2]. Medication dosage errors present in 3 of 5 sessions reinforce that caution [3].

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient AI Scribe Prototype v0.1
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician (Family Medicine), Physician (Internal Medicine), Nurse Practitioner
sources.excerpt:
[CRITICAL] (phi-handling) In 2 of 5 sessions, the prototype's draft transcript persisted in an editable state after the simulated encounter ended with no clear indication of where/how long it was stored — a potential PHI retention/audit gap that needs Security review before any real-patient pilot.
[HIGH] (accuracy) The scribe correctly captured the chief complaint and HPI in all 5 sessions but missed or garbled medication dosages in 3 of 5 — physicians said this was disqualifying for direct sign-off without review.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient AI Scribe Prototype v0.1
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician (Family Medicine), Physician (Internal Medicine), Nurse Practitioner
sources.excerpt:
[HIGH] (trust calibration) 4 of 5 participants read every line of AI-generated text before accepting it in this first exposure; none trusted it enough to skim, which undercuts the time-savings premise if that behavior persists post-adoption.
[MEDIUM] (interaction) Participants were unsure how to correct a single wrong sentence without regenerating the whole note; the edit affordance wasn't discoverable.
[MEDIUM] (workflow fit) The 'start listening' control required a manual click, which physicians said they would likely forget mid-conversation with a patient.

sources.title: The Longitudinal Physician — Ambient Scribe Journey (v0.1 to Post-GA)
sources.excerpt:
v0.1 (Feb 2025) — Skeptical, reads every generated line; medication dosage errors present in 3 of 5 sessions reinforce that caution.
v0.2 (Sep 2025) — Errors drop, but reading behavior doesn't — still reads every line despite the accuracy gain. A frustration plateau: "why doesn't this feel any different?"
GA Candidate (Jan 2026) — Per-line confidence highlighting introduces the first behavior change: begins skimming high-confidence lines for the first time. Relief, tempered by sound-alike medication names still being a known, monitored gap.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the AI's citations?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion, not just a black-box draft. [1]

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.participants: Participants: 4 — Utilization Review Nurse, Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor)

questions.question: How did new admins expect the invite step to work?

seeded.answer: Participants were unsure whether invites sent immediately or only when the setup wizard was submitted. [1] Two out of three participants tried to skip step 3 ("Connect calendar") entirely, assuming it was optional even though it's required. [1] Dana, in a storyboard, added a test email first to see what happened because she wasn't sure if invites sent immediately. [2]

sources.title: Onboarding Study — Session 1–3 Topline
sources.excerpt:
All 3 participants paused at step 4 ("Invite your team") — unsure whether invites send immediately or wait until setup is finished.
2 of 3 tried to skip step 3 ("Connect calendar") entirely, assuming it was optional even though it's required.
Nobody read the sidebar progress indicator — all navigated by scrolling.

sources.title: Dana's Monday Morning Setup
sources.excerpt:
Dana opens the signup link from an email, still reading a Slack message.
She breezes through steps 1–3 (signup, basics, calendar), barely reading.
Step 4 ("Invite your team") — she stops, phone buzzes, she hesitates before adding real emails.
She adds one test email first to see what happens (current design gives her no way to do this safely).
Relief when nothing sends immediately — but she wasn't sure until then.

questions.question: What haven't we learned yet about care coordinators?

seeded.answer:
The sources don't directly address what hasn't been learned about care coordinators.

They do show that care coordinators distrust auto-generated summaries from the EHR's AVS tool because they've caught it omitting recently changed medications. [1] They also show that care coordinators want a system that tells them what changed since they last touched a chart. [2]

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

seeded.answer:
The interaction between the session lock and an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view's own notes [1].

Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side [1]. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change [1].

IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.
